evidence: Caes. BG 4.21.5: quī polliceantur obsidēs dare
Plaut. Bacch. 185: hospitium et cēnam pollicēre
terms.comment: With a future infinitive (sē ventūrum pollicitus est), in comedy and in Caesar also a present; or with an object: operam pollicērī, to offer one’s help. The same verb serves for “promise”.

evidence: Liv. 40.23: in omnia ultrō suam offerēns operam (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: ā complūribus īnsulae cīvitātibus ad eum lēgātī veniunt, quī polliceantur obsidēs dare atque imperiō populī Rōmānī obtemperāre
phrases.english: envoys come to him from several states of the island, to offer to give hostages and to submit to the rule of the Roman people

phrases.latin: venīre tū mē gaudēs: ego crēdō tibi; hospitium et cēnam pollicēre, ut convenit peregrē advenientī
phrases.english: You’re glad I’ve come: I believe you; you offer me a bed and dinner, as is right for someone arriving from abroad

sources: Lewis & Short: polliceor · Lewis & Short: offero · Lewis & Short: opera
